concepts.title: Time and Space Complexity
objectives: Count repeated operations rather than guessing from syntax.
Separate input storage, auxiliary space and output size.
concepts.mentalModel: Treat a loop as a counter of work. Doubling the input doubles a full scan, roughly quadruples a square nested loop, and adds about one iteration to repeated halving.
concepts.workedExample: For n=8, a scan performs 8 visits, a square nested loop performs 64 visits, and repeated integer halving visits 8,4,2,1: 4 iterations. These counts describe the defined operations, not elapsed milliseconds.
concepts.invariant: The operation counter increases once for each visit of the selected loop body.
concepts.commonMistake: Two nested loops are not automatically quadratic: their bounds and dependencies determine the count. Big-O is a growth bound, not an exact runtime.

complexity.time: O(n), O(n²), O(log n) for the three loops
complexity.assumptions: n >= 0; counting loop-body visits, excluding printing.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Each halving iteration reduces the remaining scale; contrast its count with the two earlier loops.

checkpoint.question: A square nested loop visits every pair for n=4. How many visits?
checkpoint.explanation: There are 4 choices for each of two indices: 4 × 4 = 16.

visualization.manipulation: Change n to 4 or 16 and predict the counters before comparing.
visualization.limits: Nonnegative n; teaching counter only, not a runtime profiler.
gaps: No matching interactive scene exists yet. Show the authored state sequence and Java code; do not substitute another algorithm.

applications.connection: Apply counters to actual loop bodies.
Change input scale and compare growth.

concepts.title: Arrays
objectives: Read and update by index.
Traverse an array while maintaining a running result.
concepts.mentalModel: An array is a numbered row of slots. Index i selects a position, not a value; duplicate values still occupy different slots.
concepts.workedExample: For [2,1,5], visit indices 0,1,2. The running total becomes 2,3,8. An empty row has total 0.
concepts.invariant: Before index i, total equals the sum of a[0..i).
concepts.commonMistake: The last valid index is length-1. Iterating with i <= length reads beyond the array. Integer sums may overflow; use long for the accumulator.

complexity.assumptions: Non-null int array; sum accumulated in long.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Consume one slot; the accumulator now includes that slot.

checkpoint.question: After visiting indices 0 and 1 of [2,1,5], what is total?
checkpoint.explanation: Only the first two slots have been consumed: 2 + 1 = 3.

visualization.manipulation: Edit a slot or repeat a value; predict which intermediate sums change.
visualization.limits: Empty to 32 integers; values have stable slot identities.
gaps: No matching interactive scene exists yet. Show the authored state sequence and Java code; do not substitute another algorithm.

applications.connection: Record the sum at every position.
Replace a total with a minimum-so-far decision.

concepts.title: Strings
objectives: Traverse characters and distinguish positions from substrings.
Build a result without repeatedly copying an immutable string.
concepts.mentalModel: A string is an indexed sequence of text units. Reading does not mutate it; build changed text in a separate buffer.
concepts.workedExample: Read "cat" from indices 2,1,0 and append t,a,c to produce "tac". The original string remains "cat".
concepts.invariant: After k iterations, the buffer contains the final k characters in reverse order.
concepts.commonMistake: Java char indexes UTF-16 code units, not all user-perceived characters. This introductory example is restricted to ASCII; it is not a Unicode grapheme reverser.

complexity.assumptions: ASCII teaching input; StringBuilder avoids repeated string concatenation.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Append the highlighted source character; the original string stays unchanged.

checkpoint.question: After reading index 2 of "cat", what is in the output buffer?
checkpoint.explanation: The final character is t; append it first.

visualization.manipulation: Change the string and track source index separately from output length.
visualization.limits: ASCII, 0–32 characters; Unicode expansion is separate.
gaps: No matching interactive scene exists yet. Show the authored state sequence and Java code; do not substitute another algorithm.

applications.connection: Compare the same character position across strings.
Extend traversal to matching a candidate substring.

concepts.title: Hash Maps and Sets
objectives: Use a set for exact membership and a map for key-associated state.
Check previously seen values before inserting the current one.
concepts.mentalModel: A set answers whether a value has appeared. A map additionally remembers a value such as the earlier index. Hashing locates a candidate bucket; equality still decides exact membership.
concepts.workedExample: For [2,1,2], insert 2, then 1. The last 2 is already present, so a duplicate exists. Two equal values at different positions count as repetition.
concepts.invariant: Before reading position i, seen contains exactly the values at earlier positions.
concepts.commonMistake: Hash lookup is expected constant time under normal assumptions, not a universal worst-case guarantee. A Bloom filter is not a replacement for an exact set.

complexity.assumptions: Java HashSet exact integer membership; expected hashing behaviour.

lineAnnotations.explanation: A failed insertion means exact membership was already present.

checkpoint.question: Before processing the final 2 in [2,1,2], which values are in seen?
checkpoint.explanation: Both earlier values have been inserted; the set does not store duplicate entries.

visualization.manipulation: Repeat a value, change it to a new value, and compare membership checks.
visualization.limits: 0–32 integers; show exact key equality, not invented hash addresses.
gaps: No matching interactive scene exists yet. Show the authored state sequence and Java code; do not substitute another algorithm.

applications.connection: Use membership to detect repetition.
Associate each earlier value with its index.

concepts.title: Sorting and Merging
objectives: Merge two ordered sequences using two cursors.
Explain how merge sort uses this operation after recursive splitting.
concepts.mentalModel: Two sorted rows let you take the smaller front item each time. Once both fronts are ordered, the chosen value cannot be preceded by a smaller unconsumed value.
concepts.workedExample: Merge [1,4] and [2,3]: choose 1,2,3, then drain 4. Output [1,2,3,4] is ordered and contains every input occurrence.
concepts.invariant: The output prefix is sorted and contains exactly the consumed input prefixes.
concepts.commonMistake: A merge assumes both inputs are sorted. Do not quote O(n) merging as the complexity of sorting arbitrary input. Choosing the left equal key preserves cross-run stability.

complexity.time: O(n+m) merge; O(n log n) merge sort
complexity.assumptions: Both merge inputs are nondecreasing; merge-sort child lesson covers splitting.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Compare the two current fronts; advance only the cursor whose value was emitted.

checkpoint.question: Merging [1,4] and [2,3], which value follows the first 1?
checkpoint.explanation: Compare the current fronts 4 and 2; choose 2.

visualization.manipulation: Use duplicate keys and empty runs; keep element identity through merging.
visualization.limits: Sorted runs of up to 16 elements each; splitting and pivot sorting are separate child traces.
gaps: Current child traces cover whole sorting, not the two-run merge lesson input. Splits and per-merge cursor moves need refinement.

applications.connection: Merge while preserving unread input.
Combine merging with recursive divide-and-conquer.

concepts.title: Prefix Sums
objectives: Build an exclusive-prefix table.
Answer a half-open range sum using two stored values.
concepts.mentalModel: Store the sum before every boundary. The sum between two boundaries is the later prefix minus the earlier prefix.
concepts.workedExample: For [2,1,5], prefix=[0,2,3,8]. The range [1,3) sums to prefix[3]-prefix[1]=8-2=6.
concepts.invariant: prefix[i] equals the sum of the first i values; prefix[0] is zero.
concepts.commonMistake: Mixing inclusive and exclusive endpoints causes off-by-one errors. Prefix sums work with negative values; a positive-only shrinking window is a different technique.

complexity.time: O(n) build; O(1) per range query
complexity.assumptions: 0 <= left <= right <= n; long sums.

lineAnnotations.explanation: The next boundary stores the previous prefix plus one new input value.

checkpoint.question: For prefix=[0,2,3,8], which expression gives a[1..3)?
checkpoint.explanation: Subtract the sum before boundary 1 from the sum before boundary 3.

visualization.manipulation: Move either query boundary and compare the highlighted original range.
visualization.limits: 0–32 integers; half-open endpoints; long accumulation.
gaps: No matching interactive scene exists yet. Show the authored state sequence and Java code; do not substitute another algorithm.

applications.connection: Reuse preprocessing across range queries.
Combine prefix differences with hash-map counts.

concepts.title: Two Pointers
objectives: Use ordering to discard impossible pairs.
Move one pointer with a reason rather than enumerating every pair.
concepts.mentalModel: Place a cursor at each end of a sorted row. If their sum is too small, moving the right cursor left cannot help; advance the left cursor instead.
concepts.workedExample: Sorted [1,2,3,4,6,7], target=9: 1+7=8, so advance left. Then 2+7=9. The answer exists at two distinct positions.
concepts.invariant: Any pair not yet ruled out lies within the current cursor interval.
concepts.commonMistake: The ordering argument fails for unsorted input. Sort first when permitted and count that cost; sorted positions are not original indices.

complexity.assumptions: Input is already sorted; long pair sum avoids int overflow.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Move the cursor justified by sorted order and the comparison.

checkpoint.question: At values 1 and 7 with target 9, which cursor moves?
checkpoint.explanation: The sum is too small. Only advancing the left value can increase it in a sorted interval.

visualization.manipulation: Change target or repeat a value; distinguish sorted positions from original indices.
visualization.limits: Sorted integers; distinct positions; preparation cost shown separately.
gaps: Numeric sorted-pair trace only; string normalization and palindrome visuals are not implemented.

applications.connection: Move inward while applying text normalization.
Use sorted sums to discard pairs.

concepts.title: Fixed-Size Sliding Window
objectives: Reuse a fixed-length contiguous sum.
Handle all-negative inputs and reject invalid window sizes.
concepts.mentalModel: A frame holds k adjacent values. Move it right by subtracting the outgoing value and adding the incoming one.
concepts.workedExample: For [2,1,5,1,3,2] and k=3, the full-window sums are 8,7,9,6. The largest is 9.
concepts.invariant: The rolling sum equals the last min(k,right+1) values; compare with best only after a full window exists.
concepts.commonMistake: Initializing best to zero breaks all-negative arrays. This fixed-size sum supports negative values; variable-size sum shrinking needs extra assumptions.

complexity.assumptions: 1 <= k <= n; long accumulated sums.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Remove the outgoing value once the frame would exceed k elements.

checkpoint.question: A window sum of 8 loses 2 and gains 1. What is the next sum?
checkpoint.explanation: Reuse the previous total: 8 - 2 + 1 = 7.

visualization.manipulation: Edit input or k, then predict incoming/outgoing values.
visualization.limits: 1–32 integers; 1 <= k <= n; existing interactive window trace.
gaps: Existing bounded scene supports the teaching operation; broader problem-specific visuals remain Phase 2.

applications.connection: Convert a best fixed-length sum into an average.
Use the existing original numeric-window problem.

concepts.title: Variable-Size Sliding Window
objectives: Grow and shrink a contiguous range to restore a condition.
Separate a distinct-character condition from positive-sum conditions.
concepts.mentalModel: Stretch a frame while it remains valid. When a repeated character enters, remove characters from the left until the frame is valid again.
concepts.workedExample: For "abca", the frame grows through a,ab,abc. The next a forces the old a out, leaving bca. The best length stays 3.
concepts.invariant: After shrinking, all characters in the current frame are distinct.
concepts.commonMistake: Removing only once can leave a repeated character inside the frame. For minimum-length sum windows, positivity is what makes shrinking monotonic; arbitrary negatives break that proof.

complexity.assumptions: ASCII example; each character enters/leaves at most once.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Restore validity by removing as many left values as needed.

checkpoint.question: When the second b arrives in "abba", is removing only the first a enough?
checkpoint.explanation: The old b remains, so shrink again until the duplicate is removed.

visualization.manipulation: Use "abba" to expose a single-if shrinking bug.
visualization.limits: ASCII 0–32 characters; no sum-window claims for negative numbers.
gaps: No matching interactive scene exists yet. Show the authored state sequence and Java code; do not substitute another algorithm.

applications.connection: Maintain distinct characters with a membership structure.
Use positive values to justify sum-based shrinking.

concepts.title: Binary Search
objectives: Maintain an inclusive candidate interval.
Guarantee progress and distinguish exact search from insertion boundaries.
concepts.mentalModel: A comparison with the middle of an ordered row discards a whole impossible half.
concepts.workedExample: In [1,2,3,4,6,7], target 5: mid=2 gives 3, mid=4 gives 6, then mid=3 gives 4. The interval becomes empty and returns -1.
concepts.invariant: If the target exists, some occurrence remains in [low,high].
concepts.commonMistake: Using low=mid or high=mid in this inclusive version can stop progress. Exact-match search may return any duplicate occurrence; lower-bound search answers a different question.

complexity.assumptions: Sorted nondecreasing array; mid uses low+(high-low)/2.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Discard mid along with the impossible half, guaranteeing progress.

checkpoint.question: If a[mid] is smaller than target, what is the new low in this version?
checkpoint.explanation: mid has been ruled out, so advance past it.

visualization.manipulation: Try present, absent and duplicated values; show sorting as preparation.
visualization.limits: 0–32 sorted values; current trace accepts nonempty teaching input.
gaps: Existing bounded scene supports the teaching operation; broader problem-specific visuals remain Phase 2.

applications.connection: Find an exact target.
Return the first valid insertion boundary.

concepts.title: Intervals
objectives: Sort intervals by start and merge overlaps.
State whether touching endpoints count as overlap.
concepts.mentalModel: Lay closed segments on a number line. Sorted starts let you extend the latest output segment or begin a separate one.
concepts.workedExample: For [1,3],[2,6],[8,10], the second segment overlaps the first and extends its end to 6. Result: [1,6],[8,10].
concepts.invariant: Output segments are disjoint and cover exactly the processed input intervals.
concepts.commonMistake: For closed intervals [1,2] and [2,3], equality means overlap. Half-open intervals need a different convention. Never mutate caller intervals accidentally while merging.

complexity.assumptions: Valid closed [start,end] pairs; endpoints may touch; caller input preserved.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Extend the latest merged end; preserve earlier disjoint output.

checkpoint.question: With closed endpoints, do [1,2] and [2,3] merge?
checkpoint.explanation: Both contain 2, so the merged interval is [1,3].

visualization.manipulation: Move endpoints and compare touching, nested and disjoint segments.
visualization.limits: 0–16 valid closed intervals; distinguish endpoint convention.
gaps: No matching interactive scene exists yet. Show the authored state sequence and Java code; do not substitute another algorithm.

applications.connection: Merge overlaps after ordering starts.
Exploit an already ordered disjoint collection.

concepts.title: Matrices and Grid Coordinates
objectives: Distinguish row and column dimensions.
Map a cell (r,c) to (c,r) during transpose.
concepts.mentalModel: A rectangular matrix is a row of rows. Coordinates identify both a row and a column; a transpose swaps their roles.
concepts.workedExample: Transpose [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]] into [[1,4],[2,5],[3,6]]. The input is 2×3 and the output is 3×2.
concepts.invariant: Every copied source cell a[r][c] appears at out[c][r].
concepts.commonMistake: Using row count for both dimensions only works for square inputs. Reject ragged rows for this rectangular operation.

complexity.assumptions: Rectangular non-null rows; zero rows produce an empty matrix.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Move one value to the swapped row/column coordinates.

checkpoint.question: Where does source cell (1,2) go during transpose?
checkpoint.explanation: Swap the row and column coordinates.

visualization.manipulation: Use a non-square grid and follow one cell into the output.
visualization.limits: Rectangular grid up to 6×6; ragged input explicitly invalid.
gaps: No matching interactive scene exists yet. Show the authored state sequence and Java code; do not substitute another algorithm.

applications.connection: Swap coordinate roles.
Maintain four changing traversal boundaries.

concepts.title: Linked Lists
objectives: Follow node references rather than adjacent indexes.
Reverse links without losing the unprocessed suffix.
concepts.mentalModel: Each node holds a value and a reference to the next node. Move arrows, not values, when reversing the chain.
concepts.workedExample: For 4→2→7→1→3→6, first save 2, point 4 to null, then continue from 2. The final head is 6 and the chain is 6→3→1→7→2→4.
concepts.invariant: prev heads the reversed prefix; current heads the untouched suffix.
concepts.commonMistake: Overwriting current.next before saving it loses access to the remaining nodes. Equal values still have distinct node identities.

complexity.assumptions: Acyclic singly linked list; null is an empty list.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Rewire the current node after saving its original successor.

checkpoint.question: What must be saved before overwriting current.next?
checkpoint.explanation: Keep the unprocessed suffix reachable before changing the link.

visualization.manipulation: Use duplicate values and track node IDs while reversing arrows.
visualization.limits: Acyclic list; no cyclic-list claims; existing renderer needs arrow-state refinement.
gaps: Java links preserve identity; the legacy renderer still needs to display every rewired arrow.

applications.connection: Reverse arrows iteratively.
Combine node references with merging.

concepts.title: Stacks
objectives: Use last-in, first-out operations.
Handle an empty structure before removing an element.
concepts.mentalModel: A stack is a pile with one accessible end. The last item placed on top is the first removed.
concepts.workedExample: Push 4,2,7,1,3,6. Pop returns 6,3,1,7,2,4. Values below the top retain their relative order.
concepts.invariant: The top is the most recently pushed item that has not been popped.
concepts.commonMistake: A queue removes from the opposite end. Check emptiness before pop; use a Deque rather than treating sorted order as stack order.

complexity.time: O(n) for n pushes and pops; amortized O(1) per deque operation
complexity.assumptions: ArrayDeque used as an implementation, not an assessed algorithm replacement.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Remove the newest remaining value from the top.

checkpoint.question: Push 4, then 2, then 7. Which value pops first?
checkpoint.explanation: The last pushed value, 7, is on top.

visualization.manipulation: Interleave pushes and pops; attempt a pop only after checking emptiness.
visualization.limits: 0–32 values; top and empty state explicit.
gaps: Push/pop trace exists; bracket matching and per-depth minimum visuals remain future applications.

applications.connection: Match the most recent unfinished opening.
Attach a minimum summary to each depth.

concepts.title: Queues and Deques
objectives: Use first-in, first-out processing.
Distinguish a queue discipline from a deque container.
concepts.mentalModel: Join at the back and leave from the front. A deque supports both ends, so the operations you choose determine FIFO or LIFO behavior.
concepts.workedExample: Enqueue 4,2,7,1,3,6 at the back. Removing from the front returns 4,2,7,1,3,6.
concepts.invariant: The front is the earliest enqueued item that has not been removed.
concepts.commonMistake: Using removeLast after addLast turns a deque into a stack. BFS depends on FIFO; substituting the wrong removal changes exploration order.

complexity.time: O(n) total; amortized O(1) per deque operation
complexity.assumptions: Explicit addLast/removeFirst; empty removal guarded.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Remove the earliest queued value from the front.

checkpoint.question: After addLast(4), addLast(2), what does removeFirst return?
checkpoint.explanation: 4 has waited longest at the front.

visualization.manipulation: Switch removal end and explain why the behavior becomes LIFO.
visualization.limits: 0–32 values; show front/back and FIFO ordering.
gaps: FIFO is supported; deque operations at both ends and the two-stack implementation are specifications only.

applications.connection: Discard expired timestamps from the front.
Compose FIFO behavior from two LIFO structures.

concepts.title: Recursion and the Call Stack
objectives: Define a base case and a smaller subproblem.
Distinguish a suspended frame from a returned value.
concepts.mentalModel: A function leaves a frame on the call stack while a smaller call runs. Returning resumes that exact frame with its own local state.
concepts.workedExample: factorial(5) waits for factorial(4), down to factorial(0)=1. Unwinding returns 1,2,6,24,120. Each multiplication happens after the smaller call returns.
concepts.invariant: factorial(n) returns n times factorial(n-1), with factorial(0)=1.
concepts.commonMistake: A missing base case or a call that does not reduce the problem can recurse indefinitely. The call stack consumes space even when no explicit array is allocated.

complexity.assumptions: 0 <= n <= 10 for this bounded example; array-sum application uses the same base/reduction structure.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Suspend this frame, then multiply by its own n when the smaller call returns.

checkpoint.question: What is still pending when factorial(5) calls factorial(4)?
checkpoint.explanation: The caller frame must multiply the returned result by its own n=5.

visualization.manipulation: Change n and follow frame-local n separately from returned result.
visualization.limits: n=0..10; show base frame and unwind; no arbitrary own-code tracing.
gaps: Base frame and returned values need a dedicated frame view; existing authored trace is not own-code tracing.

applications.connection: Replace a loop with a base case and smaller suffix.
Revisit reversal recursively; compare extra stack use.

concepts.title: Backtracking
objectives: Explore choices recursively and restore shared state.
Snapshot a result instead of keeping an alias to the mutable path.
concepts.mentalModel: Walk a decision tree with a reusable path. Choose an item, explore descendants, then undo that choice before trying the next branch.
concepts.workedExample: For [1,2], include-first traversal records [1,2], [1], [2], []. After recording [1,2], remove 2 before exploring the branch without it.
concepts.invariant: On entering visit(i), path contains exactly the choices for indices below i.
concepts.commonMistake: Missing the undo contaminates sibling branches. Storing path itself makes every result alias one mutable list. Duplicate input values require a separate deduplication policy.

complexity.assumptions: Distinct input values; bounded teaching subset size.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Undo the last choice so the next sibling receives the parent path.

checkpoint.question: Why copy path when recording a subset?
checkpoint.explanation: Each recorded subset must remain independent of later path changes.

visualization.manipulation: Toggle an include/exclude branch and watch undo restore the parent state.
visualization.limits: Distinct values; at most 5 items in existing trace; exponential output explicit.
gaps: Existing bounded trace records choices; branch-tree layout and undo transitions need refinement.

applications.connection: Enumerate include/exclude choices.
Add a target, candidate reuse and duplicate-order control.

concepts.title: Binary Trees and Traversal
objectives: Distinguish a general binary tree from a BST.
Visit a tree in inorder or compute height from child results.
concepts.mentalModel: A binary tree node has up to two child references. Traversal chooses when to visit the node relative to those children; no ordering property is required.
concepts.workedExample: For root 4 with left subtree 2(1,3) and right subtree 7(6,null), inorder visits [1,2,3,4,6,7] and height is 3 nodes. This example is ordered, but arbitrary binary trees need not be.
concepts.invariant: inorder(node) processes every node in left subtree, then node, then right subtree.
concepts.commonMistake: Inorder output is sorted only for a valid BST. Define whether height counts nodes or edges; the empty tree has height 0 in this lesson.

complexity.space: O(h) call stack, plus O(n) output
complexity.assumptions: Acyclic tree; height counts nodes; existing interactive child demonstrates level order, not inorder.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Return from the left subtree, then visit the node before descending right.

checkpoint.question: Does inorder traversal sort every binary tree?
options: Only if the tree satisfies the BST ordering property
checkpoint.explanation: Traversal follows links; it does not rearrange arbitrary node values.

visualization.manipulation: Change a value without rewiring links to see why general inorder need not be sorted.
visualization.limits: Small acyclic tree; inorder specification separate from the existing level-order renderer.
gaps: Existing child renderer uses BST insertion and level-order traversal. It cannot accept arbitrary binary trees or demonstrate the specified inorder traversal yet.

applications.connection: Combine child results into a depth.
Choose the visit position relative to children.

concepts.title: Binary Search Trees
objectives: Insert/search using subtree ordering.
Explain why an unbalanced BST may degrade to linear height.
concepts.mentalModel: Each node splits the remaining keys: every left key is smaller and every right key is larger. Follow that decision at each level.
concepts.workedExample: Insert [8,3,10,1,6,14,4,7,13]. Inorder becomes [1,3,4,6,7,8,10,13,14]; inserting 6 again leaves the tree unchanged.
concepts.invariant: For every node, all left descendants are smaller and all right descendants are larger.
concepts.commonMistake: Checking only immediate children does not validate a whole BST. Sorted insertion can produce a chain; O(log n) requires a height assumption.

complexity.space: O(h) recursive stack; O(n) stored nodes
complexity.assumptions: Distinct keys; duplicates ignored; no balancing in this lesson.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Compare with this node and descend into the only possible insertion subtree.

checkpoint.question: After 8,3,10, where does 6 go?
checkpoint.explanation: 6 is below 8 but above 3, so it becomes the right child of 3.

visualization.manipulation: Insert sorted or repeated keys; follow comparisons and stable node IDs.
visualization.limits: 1–32 input keys; equal keys ignored; no balancing guarantee.
gaps: Existing bounded scene supports the teaching operation; broader problem-specific visuals remain Phase 2.

applications.connection: Discard one subtree after each comparison.
Propagate ancestor bounds to every descendant.

concepts.title: Heaps and Priority Queues
objectives: Maintain parent/child heap order.
Distinguish the maximum at the root from a fully sorted array.
concepts.mentalModel: A complete tree fits in an array: parent of i is (i-1)/2. In a max-heap, a new value moves up until its parent is at least as large.
concepts.workedExample: Insert [4,2,7,1,3,6]. After 7 enters, it swaps with 4; the final heap is [7,3,6,1,2,4]. Only parent-child order is guaranteed.
concepts.invariant: Every parent is at least as large as its children.
concepts.commonMistake: A heap is not a sorted array, and Java PriorityQueue defaults to a min-heap. A top-k problem needs a deliberate choice of min/max orientation.

complexity.time: O(log n) per insertion; O(n log n) repeated insertion
complexity.assumptions: Custom max-heap insertion shown; bottom-up O(n) heap building is a later extension.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Move a newly inserted value up one level while preserving the other heap entries.

checkpoint.question: Is every sibling pair ordered in a max-heap?
checkpoint.explanation: The invariant constrains parents and children, not sibling order.

visualization.manipulation: Insert a new maximum and observe every parent comparison/swap.
visualization.limits: 0–32 values; existing trace records completed insertions, intermediate bubble swaps remain a renderer/trace gap.
gaps: Trace shows completed insertions; capture/render every sift comparison and swap plus extraction before claiming full heap coverage.

applications.connection: Use a min-heap to retain the k largest stream values.
Use a max-heap for repeated largest-pair removal.

concepts.title: Graph Representation
objectives: Build an adjacency list including isolated vertices.
Distinguish directed edges, undirected edges and edge weights.
concepts.mentalModel: A graph names vertices and stores their connections. An adjacency list gives every vertex a row of outgoing neighbours, including an empty row for an isolated vertex.
concepts.workedExample: For n=4 and directed edges 0→1,0→2,2→3, adjacency is [[1,2],[],[3],[]]. Making this undirected also requires the reverse connection for each edge.
concepts.invariant: Every supplied directed edge u→v contributes v to exactly the outgoing row for u.
concepts.commonMistake: Forgetting isolated vertices changes n. A matrix costs O(V²) storage, while a list stores O(V+E). Parallel edges and self loops require an explicit policy.

complexity.assumptions: Vertices 0..n-1; directed edges; preserve parallel edges and self loops.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Add one directed outgoing neighbour without losing isolated rows.

checkpoint.question: For an undirected edge between 0 and 1, which rows need entries?
checkpoint.explanation: Store 1 under 0 and 0 under 1, unless using a different explicitly documented representation.

visualization.manipulation: Toggle directedness or add an isolated vertex, self loop or parallel edge.

concepts.title: Breadth-First Search
objectives: Use FIFO to explore by edge-distance layers.
Mark discovery on enqueue so a vertex is queued once.
concepts.mentalModel: A queue holds the discovered frontier. Removing the oldest vertex finishes the nearer layer before later discoveries.
concepts.workedExample: For the teaching graph with edges i→i+1 and i→i+2 where valid, start from 0. Queue [0] becomes [1,2], then [2,3], then [3,4]. Distances are [0,1,1,2,2,3].
concepts.invariant: When first enqueued, distance[v] is the minimum number of unweighted edges from the source.
concepts.commonMistake: Visited-on-removal can enqueue the same vertex many times. BFS does not minimize arbitrary weighted costs; unreachable vertices retain -1.

complexity.assumptions: Unweighted directed graph; valid source; neighbour order follows input.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Record discovery and distance before enqueueing, preventing duplicate queue entries.

checkpoint.question: Why mark a vertex discovered when it enters the queue?
checkpoint.explanation: Another parent can encounter it before it is removed; early discovery prevents duplicates.

visualization.manipulation: Compare queue and discovery state; change generated input length.
visualization.limits: Current trace generates a directed graph and ignores displayed weights for BFS; explicit adjacency/grid input is future work.
gaps: Generated graph only; explicit graphs, cycles, disconnected vertices and multi-source grid input need renderer/input expansion.
The current trace records processing order; shortest-edge distances are verified in the Java example but are not yet displayed per vertex.

applications.connection: Reuse FIFO for nodes grouped by depth.
Use simultaneous grid sources and layer-based minutes.

concepts.title: Depth-First Search
objectives: Explore a branch before returning to its parent.
Use a visited set to handle cycles and a forest to cover disconnected components.
concepts.mentalModel: Keep the current path on the call stack. Enter an unvisited neighbour, finish its descendants, then return to try the next neighbour.
concepts.workedExample: With neighbours in ascending order on the generated six-vertex graph, DFS enters 0,1,2,3,4,5 before unwinding. Changing neighbour order can produce a different valid DFS.
concepts.invariant: Every active frame represents a discovered vertex whose outgoing neighbours are not yet fully explored.
concepts.commonMistake: DFS does not guarantee shortest paths. Mark before descending to break cycles. Pre-marking every sibling before exploring one can produce a traversal that is not recursive DFS.

complexity.assumptions: Small teaching graphs; outer loop covers disconnected components; recursion may overflow on deep real graphs.

lineAnnotations.explanation: Suspend this frame and fully explore one unvisited neighbour before trying the next.

checkpoint.question: Does finding a vertex first with DFS prove the shortest route?
checkpoint.explanation: DFS follows a branch without maintaining distance layers.

visualization.manipulation: Step through entry and return; compare recursive path with BFS frontier.
visualization.limits: Up to 8 generated vertices; trace visits source component, full-code forest also handles disconnected graphs.
gaps: Generated graph only; explicit graphs and a visible call-frame stack remain Phase 2 work.

applications.connection: Count components across a full grid scan.
Recolour only the start component with early visited marking.

concepts.title: Dynamic Programming: Memoization and Tabulation
objectives: Define state, base cases and dependencies before coding.
Compare top-down caching with bottom-up evaluation and transfer to a new recurrence.
concepts.mentalModel: A dependency graph can revisit the same smaller question. Memoization caches answers when requested; tabulation chooses an order with dependencies already available.
concepts.workedExample: F(0)=0,F(1)=1. For n=7, both versions return 13 from table [0,1,1,2,3,5,8,13]. Staircase counts and House Robber reuse state thinking but have different meanings and base cases.
concepts.invariant: A cached state is final; a bottom-up state reads only final earlier dependencies.
concepts.commonMistake: Using zero to mean both uncomputed and a valid answer is ambiguous. Memorizing Fibonacci code does not define a state for House Robber; derive take/skip decisions for the prefix instead.

complexity.space: O(n) table; top-down also O(n) call stack
complexity.assumptions: n=0..16; examples keep table for visibility; final-value rolling storage can use O(1).

lineAnnotations.explanation: Read two final dependencies and store the destination state exactly once.

checkpoint.question: If F(4)=3 and F(5)=5, what is F(6)?
checkpoint.explanation: The recurrence reads both earlier states: 3+5=8.

visualization.manipulation: Change n, compare repeated calls with cache hits and bottom-up writes.
visualization.limits: n=0..16; do not imply Fibonacci is the complete DP curriculum; practice derives two distinct state models.
gaps: Fibonacci is supported; staircase and take/skip practice require their own state explanations and future interactive scenes.

applications.connection: Derive route-count states and correct bases.
Derive maximum-value prefix states with take/skip choices.
